newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Errant NZ Maori MP Morgan cleared of fraud.
newsitem.headline: Errant NZ Maori MP Morgan cleared of fraud.

text.p: Member of Parliament Tukoroirangi Morgan, whose blunders have triggered a series of political headaches for his Maori-dominated New Zealand First party this year, was cleared of fraud on Thursday.

Morgan, whose future as an MP was on the line ahead of Serious Fraud Office and Companies Office investigations into the affairs of pilot Maori broadcaster Aotearoa Television Network, told parliament he was glad to have been exonerated.
"We are pleased (the report) confirms that no criminal conduct was found. I appreciate this matter had been of great concern to my family, friends and the people I represent," he said.
Morgan was an executive producer and presenter at partly state-funded ATN until last October's general election.
Throughout this year, newspapers have been peppered with reports of his spending company money on expensive clothes as ATN's financial problems have been widely publicised.
These reports spurred frequent calls by opposition MPs for him to resign from parliament, while Morgan argued that he had the authority to buy such items as an NZ$89 (US$60) pair of boxer shorts.

Pending the release of the Serious Fraud Office report, Morgan managed to get deeper into hot water with a tactic unheard of New Zealand's genteel political climate -- trying to sell an exclusive interview to television news stations.
His aim was in part to help finance two libel actions in which he was embroiled.
When he tried to cover up this deal he crossed his party leader, Deputy Prime Minister and Treasurer Winston Peters, who responded by putting Morgan's status under review until today.
The SFO report concluded that the evidence "fell short of establishing any serious or complex fraud", and the Companies Office said it found no evidence that rules had been broken.

But the SFO highlighted what it called "lax arrangements" controlling the spending of ATN funds and said Morgan was one of two employees whose spending on personal clothing "was clearly disproportionate to that of the other executive producers".
It was due to the absence of any obligation to account for expenditure that the office was unable to say if any conduct was criminal, acting SFO head Judge Ron Jamieson concluded.
The legal wording of the office's conclusion left opposition MPs howling with disgust, while a triumphant Peters, a lawyer and no stranger to technicalities, lauded his man.
Speaking from Australia, Peters said Morgan had been a victim of "vicious lies and deceit", and the country had been "grievously misled" by the efforts of opposition politicians.

He declined to comment on the damage the entire affair appears to have done to NZ First's popularity, which has dropped to about five percent in opinion polls from nearer 13 in the polling booths last October.
The tales of Tuku' and his television career are unlikely to vanish from the headlines, even after these reports, however.
Morgan has one libel suit under way, against Labour MP Trevor Mallard for comments he made at a news conference about Morgan's role in ATN, and is defending himself in another case.
